title: Subdivision of finite ordered complexes as nerves of face posets
statement:
Use simplicial sets [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set] and ordinary nerves [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. For a small simplicial set $X$, define $\operatorname{Sd}X$ as the degreewise colimit [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit] over its category of simplices $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ (an arrow from $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ to $\tau:\Delta^m\to X$ is a monotone map $\alpha:[n]\to[m]$ with $\tau\circ\Delta(\alpha)=\sigma$) of $N(\mathcal P_+([n]))$, where $\mathcal P_+([n])$ is the poset of nonempty subsets of $[n]$ ordered by inclusion; a monotone map acts by image of subsets. Define $(\operatorname{Ex}Y)_n=\operatorname{Hom}(N(\mathcal P_+([n])),Y)$, with simplex operators given by precomposition with the subset-image maps. There is a natural bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}(\operatorname{Sd}X,Y)\cong\operatorname{Hom}(X,\operatorname{Ex}Y).$$
The natural maps $\lambda_X:\operatorname{Sd}X\to X$ induced on each simplex by taking largest vertices transpose to $j_X:X\to\operatorname{Ex}X$, whose value on a simplex $\sigma$ is $\sigma\lambda_{\Delta^n}$.

Let $P$ be a finite poset and let $\mathcal F$ be a collection of nonempty chains in $P$, closed under taking nonempty subsets. Let $A$ be the simplicial subset of $N(P)$ consisting of weakly increasing sequences whose sets of vertices belong to $\mathcal F$. Regard $\mathcal F$ as a poset under inclusion. There is a canonical isomorphism $\operatorname{Sd}A\cong N(\mathcal F)$. Under this isomorphism $\lambda_A$ sends a chain $F_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_r$ to the weakly increasing sequence $(\max F_0,\ldots,\max F_r)$. Let $P'$ be another finite poset, let $\mathcal F'$ be a collection of nonempty chains in $P'$ closed under taking nonempty subsets, and define $A'\subseteq N(P')$ from $\mathcal F'$ by the same weakly increasing sequence rule. If $u:P\to P'$ is monotone and $u(F)\in\mathcal F'$ for every $F\in\mathcal F$, the corresponding map $\operatorname{Sd}A\to\operatorname{Sd}A'$ is the nerve of $F\mapsto u(F)$. These identifications include empty complexes and are compatible with inclusions of subcomplexes. In particular, for every finite poset $P$, $\operatorname{Sd}N(P)\cong N(\operatorname{Ch}(P))$, where $\operatorname{Ch}(P)$ is the poset of nonempty chains in $P$ ordered by inclusion.

Online sources read 2026-10-17; archive WANTED.

proof.text: Write $B_n=N(\mathcal P_+([n]))$. By the nerve definition [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], an $r$-simplex of $B_n$ is a flag $T_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq T_r$ of nonempty subsets. A monotone $\alpha:[n]\to[m]$ sends it to $(\alpha(T_0),\ldots,\alpha(T_r))$. Images are nonempty, preserve inclusions, and satisfy $(\beta\alpha)(T)=\beta(\alpha(T))$, so these formulas define a functor $B:\Delta\to\mathrm{sSet}$. Precomposition with $B(\alpha)$ therefore gives the asserted simplicial operators on $\operatorname{Ex}Y$. Also, a simplex $x\in X_n$ defines $\sigma_x:\Delta^n\to X$ by $\sigma_x(\beta)=X(\beta)(x)$; conversely a simplicial map $\sigma$ is determined by $x=\sigma(\mathrm{id}_{[n]})$, since its naturality forces this formula [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set].

proof.text:
Use the following concrete model for the degreewise colimit. In degree $r$ take the disjoint union of pairs $(\sigma,T_\bullet)$, with $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ and $T_\bullet\in(B_n)_r$, modulo the equivalence relation generated by
$$(\tau\Delta(\alpha),T_\bullet)\sim(\tau,\alpha(T_\bullet)).$$
The indexing category is small: its objects form $\coprod_{n\geq0}X_n$, and its arrows are subsets of the sets of monotone maps between finite ordinals. Restricting a flag along $\theta:[s]\to[r]$ commutes with every subset-image map, hence descends to the quotient and satisfies the simplicial identities. Write $[\sigma,T_\bullet]$ for its classes. For any compatible family of maps out of the $B_n$, its value on a class must be its value on the representative; compatibility makes this well-defined, and representatives exhaust the quotient. This verifies, rather than assumes, the universal property [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit], also for simplicial maps because the same formula commutes with restrictions [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set].

source.place: Proposition 3.3.3.3 and Corollary 3.3.3.4 (00Y9), quotient construction of subdivision; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: Let $\iota_\sigma:B_n\to\operatorname{Sd}X$ send a flag to its class. Given $f:\operatorname{Sd}X\to Y$, define $g_n(x)=f\iota_{\sigma_x}\in\operatorname{Hom}(B_n,Y)$. For $\alpha:[m]\to[n]$, the quotient relation gives $\iota_{\sigma_x\Delta(\alpha)}=\iota_{\sigma_x}B(\alpha)$, which is exactly the operator equation $g_m(X(\alpha)x)=g_n(x)B(\alpha)$. Thus $g:X\to\operatorname{Ex}Y$ is simplicial [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set]. Conversely a simplicial $g$ assigns $g_n(x):B_n\to Y$ to each $\sigma_x$; that same operator equation is the cocone compatibility required by [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit], so it induces $f$ with $f_r[\sigma_x,T_\bullet]=(g_n(x))_r(T_\bullet)$.

source.place: Corollary 3.3.3.4, explicit two directions of the Hom bijection; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: Starting from $f$, the reconstructed map has value $f_r[\sigma,T_\bullet]$ on every representative and hence equals $f$. Starting from $g$, evaluating the reconstructed map on $\iota_{\sigma_x}$ returns exactly $g_n(x)$. The two assignments are therefore inverse. For $h:X'\to X$, subdivision sends $[\sigma,T_\bullet]$ to $[h\sigma,T_\bullet]$, and for $k:Y\to Y'$ the other operation is postcomposition with $k$. Write $\Theta_{X,Y}(f)=g$ for the assignment of step 3. For $x\in X_n^{\prime}$, the representatives give $\sigma_{h_n(x)}=h\sigma_x$ and $\operatorname{Sd}(h)\iota_{\sigma_x}=\iota_{h\sigma_x}$, so $(\Theta_{X^{\prime},Y}(f\operatorname{Sd}(h)))_n(x)=f\iota_{h\sigma_x}=(\Theta_{X,Y}(f))_n(h_n(x))$. For $x\in X_n$, $(\Theta_{X,Y^{\prime}}(kf))_n(x)=kf\iota_{\sigma_x}=k((\Theta_{X,Y}(f))_n(x))$. These are the two naturality equations; the inverse bijection obeys them as well by the inverse identities just proved.

proof.text:
The map $M_n:\mathcal P_+([n])\to[n]$, $T\mapsto\max T$, is monotone. For every monotone $\alpha$ one has $\max\alpha(T)=\alpha(\max T)$, since $\alpha(\max T)$ belongs to $\alpha(T)$ and bounds all of it. Taking nerves gives maps $\lambda_n:B_n\to\Delta^n$; here $N([n])=\Delta^n$ because both have weakly increasing maps $[r]\to[n]$ as their $r$-simplices [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Consequently the maps $\sigma\lambda_n$ satisfy the quotient relation and induce $\lambda_X$ by [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. On representatives its formula is
$$(\lambda_X)_r[\sigma,T_\bullet]=\sigma_r(\max T_0,\ldots,\max T_r).$$
Postcomposing $\sigma$ by any $h:X\to X'$ commutes with this formula, so $\lambda$ is natural.

proof.text: For $X=\Delta^n$, each simplex $\beta:\Delta^m\to\Delta^n$ is an arrow to $\mathrm{id}_{\Delta^n}$ in its simplex category, so the quotient relation gives $[\beta,T_\bullet]=[\mathrm{id}_{\Delta^n},\beta(T_\bullet)]$. Conversely $[\beta,T_\bullet]\mapsto\beta(T_\bullet)$ respects all relations. These are inverse identifications $\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\cong B_n$, under which $\lambda_{\Delta^n}=\lambda_n$. Apply step 3 to $f=\lambda_X$: its transpose sends $\sigma:\Delta^n\to X$ to $\lambda_X\iota_\sigma=\sigma\lambda_n$. This is precisely the asserted $j_X$ formula, including naturality by step 4 and the preceding step.

source.place: Construction 3.3.4.3, transpose and normalization on a standard simplex; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: Now fix $P,\mathcal F,A$ as in the statement. Regard a poset as the category with a unique arrow $p\to q$ when $p\leq q$; its nerve consists of weakly increasing sequences [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. The support of any restriction of such a sequence is a nonempty subset of its original support. The downward-closure hypothesis on $\mathcal F$ thus makes $A$ a simplicial subset [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set]. In particular, every simplex $\sigma:[n]\to P$ of $A$ has nonempty chain support $H=\sigma([n])\in\mathcal F$, and every nonempty $T\subseteq[n]$ has $\sigma(T)\in\mathcal F$. Every $F\in\mathcal F$ has its unique strictly increasing enumeration $e_F:[|F|-1]\to P$, whose support is $F$, so it too is a simplex of $A$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.3.17, ordered-complex special case: explicit supports and face enumerations; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text:
Define $\Phi_r:(\operatorname{Sd}A)_r\to N(\mathcal F)_r$ on representatives by
$$\Phi_r[\sigma,T_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq T_r]=(\sigma(T_0)\subseteq\cdots\subseteq\sigma(T_r)).$$
Step 7 proves membership in $\mathcal F$ and inclusion follows from images of subsets. For each generating relation of step 2, $(\tau\alpha)(T_k)=\tau(\alpha(T_k))$ for every $k$, so the two representatives have the same image. Selecting or repeating entries of a flag selects or repeats the same image entries. Thus $\Phi$ is a well-defined simplicial map to the nerve [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]; no comparison theorem for general simplicial sets has been used.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.3.17 and Example 3.3.3.18 (00YM), forward map on representatives; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text:
For an $r$-simplex $F_0\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_r$ of $N(\mathcal F)$, enumerate its largest face by $e=e_{F_r}:[d]\to P$, and put $I_k=e^{-1}(F_k)$. These are nonempty nested subsets of $[d]$, with $I_r=[d]$. Define the degreewise reverse function by
$$\Psi_r(F_\bullet)=[e_{F_r},I_\bullet].$$
Its definition uses only the unique ordering on the finite chain $F_r$. Since $e_{F_r}(I_k)=F_k$, the formula for $\Phi$ immediately gives $\Phi_r\Psi_r=1$.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.3.17, explicit reverse map for an ordered complex; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text:
To check the other composite, start with $[\sigma,T_\bullet]$ and let $H=\sigma([n])$. Write $e_H:[m]\to P$ for its increasing enumeration and $q:[n]\to[m]$ for the unique map with $e_Hq=\sigma$. It is monotone: $\sigma(a)\leq\sigma(b)$ for $a\leq b$, and $e_H$ lists $H$ in order. It is surjective by the definition of $H$. The arrow $q:\sigma\to e_H$ in the simplex category gives
$$[\sigma,T_\bullet]=[e_H,q(T_\bullet)].$$
This is the explicit removal of repeated vertices; no general unique-degeneracy theorem is needed.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.3.17, direct compression of a possibly degenerate simplex; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: Put $G=\sigma(T_r)\in\mathcal F$ and let $a:[d]\to[m]$ be the injection listing $e_H^{-1}(G)$. Then $e_Ha=e_G$. Each $q(T_k)$ is contained in $q(T_r)=e_H^{-1}(G)$, so $J_k=a^{-1}(q(T_k))$ is nonempty and $a(J_k)=q(T_k)$. The arrow $a:e_G\to e_H$ gives $[e_H,q(T_\bullet)]=[e_G,J_\bullet]$. Moreover $J_k=e_G^{-1}(\sigma(T_k))$ because $e_H$ is injective. This last representative is exactly $\Psi_r\Phi_r[\sigma,T_\bullet]$. Thus $\Psi_r\Phi_r=1$; together with step 9 this proves degreewise bijectivity of $\Phi$. For an operator $\theta:[s]\to[r]$ and a flag $F_\bullet$, simpliciality of $\Phi$ and the inverse identities give $\Phi_s((\operatorname{Sd}A)(\theta)\Psi_r(F_\bullet))=N(\mathcal F)(\theta)(F_\bullet)=\Phi_s(\Psi_s(N(\mathcal F)(\theta)(F_\bullet)))$. Injectivity of $\Phi_s$ gives the operator equation for $\Psi$. Hence $\Phi$ is the asserted simplicial isomorphism.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.3.17, restriction to the largest image face and inverse check; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: Evaluate $\lambda_A$ on the representative $[e_{F_r},e_{F_r}^{-1}(F_\bullet)]$ of step 9. The formula of step 5 gives the sequence with $k$th entry $e_{F_r}(\max e_{F_r}^{-1}(F_k))=\max F_k$, since $e_{F_r}$ is increasing. These entries form a weakly increasing sequence because $F_k\subseteq F_{k+1}$ and both lie in the chain $F_r$; its support is a nonempty subset of $F_r$, so it belongs to $A$. This proves exactly the displayed last-vertex formula under the face-poset isomorphism.

source.place: Construction 3.3.4.3, last-vertex formula on the explicit inverse representatives; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: Let $u:P\to P'$ satisfy the stated hypothesis. Applying $u$ entrywise carries each simplex of $A$ into $A'$, since its image support is $u(H)\in\mathcal F'$. The function $\mathcal F\to\mathcal F'$, $F\mapsto u(F)$, is monotone for inclusion, even if $u$ identifies vertices. Subdivision sends $[\sigma,T_\bullet]$ to $[u\sigma,T_\bullet]$, and $\Phi'$ sends that to $(u(\sigma(T_0)),\ldots,u(\sigma(T_r)))$. This equals the entrywise nerve map of $F\mapsto u(F)$ after $\Phi$ [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Representatives exhaust subdivision, so the two maps are equal. Taking $u$ to be the identity and $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathcal F'$ proves compatibility with inclusions of subcomplexes (and also with inclusions into a larger vertex poset).

source.place: Remark 3.3.3.21, explicit image-of-faces rule including collapse of vertices; explicit agent argument from the definitions, online sources read 2026-10-17; local Kerodon archive WANTED.

proof.text: If $\mathcal F=\varnothing$, there are no simplices in $A$, the disjoint unions in step 2 are empty, and $N(\mathcal F)$ is empty in every degree. Thus the construction gives the unique empty-to-empty isomorphism; no enumeration of an empty face was invoked. This also covers $P=\varnothing$. Finally take $\mathcal F$ to be all nonempty chains in $P$. Then every weakly increasing sequence of $P$ belongs to $A=N(P)$, and the inclusion poset $\mathcal F$ is exactly $\operatorname{Ch}(P)$. Substituting into the established isomorphism yields $\operatorname{Sd}N(P)\cong N(\operatorname{Ch}(P))$, with all the previously checked formulas.
